items.t: AT&T stock: New Plano headquarters breaks ground
sum: AT&T broke ground on its new global headquarters in Plano, Texas, on Thursday, November 12, marking the start of construction with the installation of the campus's first fiber connection. The company described the project as a long-term investment in North Texas in a company announcement.

AT&T said the seven-building campus will span 54 acres and 2.2 million square feet. It is intended to bring the company's Dallas-Fort Worth teams together and provide fiber, 5G and a working cell tower for the site and the surrounding community.

The company expects to welcome its first employees to the new campus in the second half of 2028. AT&T has called North Texas home since 2008, and the project links its future workplace plans with continued investment in connectivity and employee facilities.

sum: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

AT&T’s dividend check landed on Nov. 2: $0.2775 a share, the same amount it has paid every quarter since the spring of 2022. On Tuesday the 10-year Treasury yield closed at about 5% after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report, within a hair of AT&T’s 5.1% dividend yield. If the check is part of what you live on, the question is how safe it is now.

Take a couple, 61 and 59, a scenario built for this story. They retired three years ago from software jobs, moved to Washington State, and hold 10,000 AT&T shares in a taxable brokerage account, bought on Jan. 4, 2016, at $34.35, for $343,500. The shares are worth $219,400 today. The checks are why they kept them: $2,775 every quarter, $11,100 a year, beside $1.6 million in IRAs and 401(k)s and about $200,000 in a money market fund.

The company’s own words, from its Oct. 21 third-quarter report, are that it “plans to maintain its current annualized common stock dividend of $1.11 per share” while buying back about $10 billion of stock this year. That buyback reads as the cushion under the check, and the clearest sign the dividend is safe: AT&T is spending more on its own shares in 2026 than it pays in dividends, and buybacks can be slowed before a dividend is touched. The limit of that reading is the $150 billion of net debt, which gets paid before either.

Their first check, in January 2016, was $0.48 a share, or $4,800, and AT&T raised it a penny a year to $0.52. Then, on Feb. 1, 2022, with the WarnerMedia spin-off, the board set the annual dividend at $1.11 a share, down from $2.08. For the couple that meant $20,800 a year became $11,100, a cut of $9,700 a year. Over the 19 reduced checks since, the cut has cost them $46,075.

Each AT&T share came with 0.241917 shares of Warner Bros. Discovery, 2,419 shares in their case, and they sold them the week they arrived, at $24.78, for $59,943. Add that to the 44 checks since 2016, $178,725 in dividends, and $238,668 of cash has come back on a $343,500 purchase, with $219,400 of stock still in the account: a 33% total return over nearly eleven years. The S&P 500 did far better, and they know it. The check is the point.

sum: Verizon Communications Inc. VZ has increased 14.7% in a year compared with the Wireless National industry’s growth of 105.6%. The stock has outformed the Zacks Computer & Technology sector during this period.
The company has outperformed its peers like AT&T Inc. T and T-Mobile US, Inc. TMUS. Shares of AT&T have declined 12.9%, while T-Mobile has declined 21.3% during this period.

AI infrastructure represents an emerging source of revenue diversification for Verizon. The company has signed a dark fiber agreement worth more than $2 billion with Amazon Web Services (AWS), building on its earlier agreement with Google to connect AI data centers. Management disclosed approximately $4 billion in signed contracts, supported by growing demand from hyperscalers, neocloud providers and enterprise customers.

Intensifying competition in the U.S. wireless and broadband markets remains a significant concern for Verizon. The company faces strong competition from AT&T, T-Mobile and cable operators, which continue to use competitive pricing, promotional incentives and bundled offerings to attract subscribers. Although Verizon has recently improved customer acquisition and retention metrics, sustaining subscriber growth without increasing promotional spending will be important. Its strategy of competing through network quality, customer experience and value-added services rather than aggressive price discounts could help protect margins. However, competitors adopting similar convergence strategies or increasing promotional activity could put pressure on Verizon's subscriber growth and pricing flexibility.

Weakness in equipment revenue is another challenge for the company. While mobility and broadband service revenue increased 2.9% year over year to $23.5 billion in the third quarter, lower equipment sales limited overall revenue growth. Total revenue increased just 1.5% to $34.3 billion, as equipment revenue declined 9% year over year. Management attributed the decline primarily to a reduction in wireless device upgrade activity, with postpaid upgrade volumes falling 20.3% from the prior-year quarter.
Verizon's substantial investment requirements and elevated debt remain important considerations.

sum: Grupo Televisa returned to attributable profit in the third quarter, while revenue declined as the satellite business continued to contract. The company also advanced its planned acquisition of AT&T Mexico, giving investors two competing themes: improving reported profitability and a major increase in telecommunications exposure.

In its October 29, 2026 results release, Grupo Televisa reported revenue of 14,077.7 million Mexican pesos for the quarter ended September 30, down 3.8% from 14,627.0 million pesos a year earlier. Net income attributable to the company's stockholders was 882.7 million pesos, compared with a loss of 1,932.5 million pesos in the third quarter of 2025.

The earnings recovery was not driven by stronger top-line momentum alone. Grupo Televisa said the change reflected a 407.0 million peso reduction in net finance expense and a 2,885.1 million peso decrease in income taxes. Operating income nevertheless fell 26.7% to 680.9 million pesos, after other expense increased to 969.5 million pesos from 43.7 million pesos. The company attributed the higher other expense mainly to a non-cash impairment of technical equipment, increased legal and financial advisory expenses, and the absence of a prior-year insurance claim recovery.

Operating segment income rose 5.6% to 5,996.0 million pesos, lifting the margin to 42.6% from 38.8%. Grupo Televisa linked the improvement to efficiency measures and operating expense reductions. Enterprise Services revenue increased 6.8% to 1,147.8 million pesos, while Residential Services revenue was essentially flat at 10,566.0 million pesos.

Satellite Services remained the main drag. Revenue fell 20.5% to 2,363.9 million pesos, and the business recorded 250.6 thousand net revenue-generating-unit disconnections during the quarter, primarily from 231.0 thousand video units. The release showed 2.9 million satellite units at September 30, compared with 4.1 million a year earlier.

Residential operations added 125.1 thousand units in the quarter. Broadband additions, voice growth and mobile gains more than offset 48.1 thousand video losses. Grupo Televisa also upgraded more than 1.3 million homes to fiber-to-the-home during the quarter, supporting its effort to shift the customer mix toward broadband and mobile services.

Why AT&T Stock Slumped in October
sum: A large and very well-capitalized conglomerate was bulking up its telecom assets in October, and investors felt this didn't bode well for the sector's incumbents. One that got dinged by Mr. Market was AT&T (NYSE:T), which saw its share price erode by more than 14% largely due to these fears. Even the company's estimates-beating third-quarter results, published mid-month, couldn't halt this slide.

That ambitious conglomerate is none other than the Elon Musk-led space/telecom/artificial intelligence (AI) company Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), or SpaceX. Its current revenue powerhouse is its Starlink telecom division, and, sensibly enough, management is aiming to bolster this business.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

On Oct. 8, SpaceX announced it had signed a definitive agreement with investment firm Grain Management to acquire up to 14 megahertz of low-band wireless spectrum. The financial particulars were not disclosed. On top of that, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved the company's application for its Gen2 satellite constellation. Both position SpaceX to continue expanding into a vertically integrated consumer wireless business, building on its roots as a high-data-transmission broadband purveyor.

Two weeks later, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX was planning to secure at least 80,000 cell sites in the U.S. Citing unidentified "people familiar with the matter," the financial news agency wrote that the company was in discussions with at least one wireless infrastructure business to help it with this goal. A sprawling network of cell sites would be foundational for a company aiming to become a nationwide wireless carrier.

So it's understandable that AT&T investors (and those of fellow incumbents Verizon (NYSE:VZ) and T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS)) were spooked by these developments. Mobile telephony can be a very lucrative business. Still, it isn't an easy one, and the entry of a huge and determined competitor threatens to rock the boat — at least eventually.

Why Did T-Mobile Stock Jump?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

T-Mobile US (TMUS) shares gained 6.2% on Friday, October 30, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 1.8%. The company released no announcements, earnings reports, or filings that day. A news report linked the gain to fresh estimates of what it could cost SpaceX to build a rival U.S. mobile carrier. Why would SpaceX’s plans matter to T-Mobile?

SpaceX is weighing an entry into the U.S. mobile market where T-Mobile operates. That potential entry has hung over wireless stocks, one article said on October 30. Another article that day said higher cost estimates for the project were lifting the carriers SpaceX hopes to challenge, with T-Mobile among them.
T-Mobile has already ruled out one way in. On its October 28 earnings call, management said it sees no room for SpaceX to run a mobile service on T-Mobile’s network.

SpaceX would compete for the customers T-Mobile counted in that day’s report. During the third quarter of 2026, the company added 274,000 postpaid accounts. Management calls these monthly-bill customers the all-important part of its business, and its postpaid service revenue grew 9% from a year earlier. The shares slipped 0.5% in the session after that report.

T-Mobile moved with its peers and against the market. AT&T, Verizon, Comcast, Charter and Telephone and Data Systems, the companies on its Trefis peer list, all rose in the same session, with Comcast up 4.3% and AT&T up 2.3%. The SPDR fund that tracks its sector, communication services, fell 1.3%.

No session in the prior 365 days brought T-Mobile a rise this large. The latest big move went the other way: a 7.7% fall on October 23, which left the shares at $146.54, their lowest close of the past year. That fall came after a report that SpaceX was seeking at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites to build a rival carrier.

sum: AT&T (T) is up 4.4% over the last five trading days, while the S&P 500 is down 1.1%. Strength in a weak tape pulls money in. That five-day move is not the question. The question is what holding AT&T does to your money when the market moves, because over the past year it has tended to go the other way.

On days the S&P 500 fell over the past year, AT&T moved about 55% of the index’s move in the opposite direction, so it tended to rise when the market fell. On the market’s up days, it moved about 50% of the index’s move the other way and tended to fall. That is a cushion on the bad days and a drag on the good ones, and a one-year reading can shift.

The ride is not quiet. Over the past five years, AT&T ran 24.7% annualized volatility against 17.2% for the S&P 500. Across those five years the link between the two was weakly positive. AT&T’s daily moves had a correlation of only 0.17 with the index, so most of that swing is its own.

That is a slow business, and the market prices it as one. Revenue over the trailing twelve months grew 2.6% against 8.3% for the median S&P 500 company, and the stock trades at 8.6 times earnings against a median of 22.5.

Most of the free cash AT&T generates goes back out. Management expects to return about $18 billion to shareholders in 2026 through dividends and buybacks, essentially all of the free cash flow it expects for the year.

Not quite. Over the past five years, AT&T returned 11.2% a year against 12.7% for the S&P 500, with more volatility. What you got instead was a return on its own schedule across those five years and, over the past year, a holding that tended to rise when the index fell.

sum: Its five-year correlation to the index is low enough that most of its return has been its own story, and over the past year it has tended to move opposite the market.

AT&T (T) stock was up nearly 11% over the course of a week before correcting nearly 3% yesterday. On the other hand, S&P 500 is down over the same stretch, a window that also takes in AT&T’s June-quarter results. A holding that rises while the index falls is tempting, but one week of prices proves nothing about how a stock behaves. The question that decides what this position does to your money is how much of its return is genuinely its own rather than the market you already own through an index fund and what it does to the swings in everything else.

Over the past five years AT&T stock has carried a correlation to the S&P 500 of 0.18. A reading of 1.0 would mean perfect lockstep with the index; 0 would mean unrelated moves. At 0.18, most of what these shares have done has been their own story, which is the defining trait of a genuine portfolio diversifier. It compounded while doing it, at 9.2% a year over that five-year window against 12.7% for the S&P 500, and at an annualized volatility of 25% versus 17.1% for the index. Over those same five years the two assets people reach for instead did this: gold returned 17.0% a year at a correlation to AT&T of just 0.03, while the VNQ real estate index returned 2.9% at a correlation of 0.34. Gold did better on both counts over that stretch; the point is that this stock is a third, largely independent return stream, not a substitute for either.

AT&T bets big on new tactic to keep customers from switching
sum: AT&T is continuing to see a concerning pattern of customer behavior amid tougher competition from its top rivals. As a result, the phone carrier is betting big on a bold strategy to retain its customers.
In its latest earnings report, AT&T revealed that it added 421,000 new postpaid phone customers in the fourth quarter of 2025.
However, its postpaid phone churn, the rate of customers who disconnected their phone service, reached 0.98%, reflecting an increase of 13 basis points, compared to the same time period in 2024.

AT&T also appears to be facing headwinds in its prepaid wireless business. During the quarter, it lost 255,000 prepaid phone customers, pushing its churn in the segment to 2.89%, an increase of 16 basis points year over year.

The increased loss of loyal phone customers comes after AT&T decreased its autopay discount in April last year for customers who pay their monthly bill with a debit card from $10 to $5. It also completely removed that discount for customers who pay with a credit card.

AT&T also faced sharp criticism last year for allegedly surprising customers with higher-than-expected monthly bills after getting them to switch from rival phone carriers with the promise of generous discounts.
In December, AT&T also raised its Administrative & Regulatory Cost Recovery fee from $3.49 to $3.99 per line, a charge that phone customers pay on their monthly bills.

items.t: AT&T's Lumen Deal Hides an Opportunity Most Investors Are Missing
sum: Telecom giant AT&T (NYSE: T) agreed to pay $5.75 billion last year to acquire Lumen's fiber business. The deal, which is expected to close early this year, will add 4 million passed locations and 1 million subscribers to AT&T's growing fiber network.

Once the deal is closed, AT&T plans to sell a partial ownership stake in the newly created subsidiary that will hold these assets. The subsidiary will then operate as a commercial open-access platform, with AT&T as the anchor tenant. This approach will help AT&T keep its debt levels down.

What AT&T won't be able to avoid are meaningful integration costs, with earnings taking a hit in the near term. However, the company expects the long-term opportunity to be more than worth the cost.

AT&T expects its adjusted earnings per share in 2026 to be negatively impacted by about $0.05 by integration costs and additional interest expenses related to the Lumen deal and its agreement to buy spectrum licenses from EchoStar. In the first quarter of 2026, there will be some additional costs related to integrating and scaling Lumen's retail operations.

Much of the cost associated with integrating Lumen will be incurred this year, but there will also be an impact over the next few years. AT&T CFO Pasal Desroches noted in the earnings call that "We're going to incur pretty significant acquisition initial cost to integrate those assets. And to build this and to add to the distribution behind them." However, he expects those costs to moderate over the next two to three years.

In the first quarter of 2026, EBITDA and free cash flow are expected to be weak, partly due to the necessary Lumen-related investments. EBITDA is expected to expand by 3% to 4% in 2026, with growth accelerating to 5% or better in 2028.
